title: Climate
summary: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a small area at a point of time and changes often; climate is the sum total of weather conditions over a large area for a long period (more than 30 years). India has a monsoon climate.

1. Location (latitude): places nearer the equator are hotter. The Tropic of Cancer divides India into a tropical south and a sub-tropical north. 2. Distance from the sea: coastal areas have an equable climate; interior places like Delhi have an extreme climate. 3. Altitude: temperature falls with height — Shimla is cooler than Ludhiana. 4. Mountain ranges: the Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds and make the monsoon winds shed rain in India; the Western Ghats cause heavy rain on their western slopes. 5. Surface winds: in winter winds blow from land to sea (cold, dry); in summer from sea to land (moist, rain-bearing). 6. Upper-air currents: jet streams blow at about 12,000 m; in winter they bring western disturbances from the Mediterranean that give rain to north-west India, and their northward shift in summer helps the onset of the monsoon.

'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mausim', meaning season — a seasonal reversal of wind direction. In summer intense heat over north-west India (45–47°C) creates a low-pressure 'monsoon trough' from Jaisalmer to Balasore, while the Indian Ocean is cooler with high pressure. Winds blow from the sea towards the land from the south-west, opposite to the winter north-east trade winds. Being moisture-laden, they give 80–90% of India's annual rain between June and September.

Characteristics: monsoons are irregular and uncertain (early or late); rainfall is unequally distributed (Kerala, West Bengal and Odisha get heavy rain, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh less); the sudden heavy onset is the 'burst of the monsoon', mainly on the Kerala coast; there are 'breaks' — wet and dry spells.

(a) Cold weather season (December–February): temperature decreases from south to north (12–15°C in the north, about 25°C in the south); frost in the north-west; light rain from western disturbances helps rabi crops; snow on the Himalayas. North-east trade winds blow from land to sea, so the season is dry — except the Tamil Nadu coast, where these winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and give winter rain.

(b) Hot weather season (March–May): high temperatures in the plains, west and central India; the monsoon trough forms; hot, dry 'loo' winds blow over the northern plains; dust storms in the north-west; violent thunderstorms called 'Kaal Baisakhi' in West Bengal; pre-monsoon 'mango showers' in Kerala and Karnataka help mangoes ripen.

(c) Advancing south-west monsoon season (June–September): winds from the south-west reach the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in late May and the Kerala coast in the first week of June. The Arabian Sea branch, blocked by the Western Ghats, gives heavy rain on their western side and reaches Mumbai by 10 June; the Deccan beyond is a rain-shadow area. The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the north-east and West Bengal and turns west along the plains, with rain decreasing westward (Kolkata 120 cm, Allahabad 91 cm, Delhi 56 cm). The whole country is covered by 15 July. Floods and droughts occur.

(d) Retreating monsoon season (October–November): the monsoon withdraws; hot and humid 'October heat' in the north; the low pressure shifts to the Bay of Bengal, producing tropical cyclones that hit Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, especially the Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna deltas.

Rainfall is very uneven: it decreases from east to west in the northern plains and from the coast to the interior in the peninsula, and increases with altitude in the north-east. Heavy (over 200 cm): the west coast, sub-Himalayan north-east and the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya. Moderate (100–200 cm): parts of the Western Ghats, West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar. Low (60–100 cm): parts of UP, Rajasthan and the interior Deccan. Inadequate (below 60 cm): western Rajasthan, Gujarat, Ladakh and the south-central part. India has both one of the rainiest and one of the driest places in the world.

Agriculture follows the seasons: kharif crops are sown with the monsoon, rabi crops in winter and zaid crops at the end of winter. Festivals match harvests and seasons — Makar Sankranti, Lohri and Pongal in January, Basant Panchami, Holi and Baisakhi, Onam in Kerala, Dussehra, Durga Puja and Diwali after the monsoon. Urbanisation, industrialisation, deforestation and burning fossil fuels raise CO2 and CFCs; these greenhouse gases trap heat (global warming), disturbing the cycle of seasons and threatening agriculture, on which about 70% of Indians depend.

Answer briefly: (a) Why does Meghalaya receive more than 200 cm of rainfall per year? (b) Why does Rajasthan receive less than 60 cm of rainfall per year?

(a) The moist Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon is trapped by the funnel-shaped Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills and forced to rise, giving very heavy rain. vsa: Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers towards the end of the hot season, especially in Kerala and Karnataka. They help in the early ripening of mangoes, hence the name.
Explain any two features of the monsoon in India.

(1) Monsoons are irregular — they may come early or late and are affected by regional conditions. (2) Rainfall is unequal — coastal areas like Kerala and West Bengal get heavy rain while interior regions get less; the sudden heavy onset is called the 'burst of the monsoon'.

Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a small area at a particular time and can change within a day. Climate is the average weather of a large area over a long period (over 30 years) and generally does not change.
What are jet streams? How are they significant for change of weather in India?

Jet streams are narrow belts of very fast upper-air winds at about 12,000 m. In winter they bring western disturbances (from the Mediterranean) that give rain to north-west India; in summer they shift north over Central Asia, which helps the onset of the monsoon.
What type of weather prevails during October in different parts of India?

October is the retreating monsoon season. In the northern plains the weather is hot and humid ('October heat') but nights become pleasant by the end of the month; on the east coast cyclones from the Bay of Bengal bring heavy rain to Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
sa: What makes the Indian monsoon unique? Mention any three features.

(1) It is a seasonal reversal of winds — south-west in summer and north-east in winter. (2) It is irregular: its arrival, amount and withdrawal vary, and it has 'breaks' with wet and dry spells. (3) It begins with a sudden 'burst' on the Kerala coast and is unequally distributed, giving 80–90% of India's rain in four months (June–September).

Why does the Tamil Nadu coast receive rainfall during winter while most of India remains dry? Explain two reasons.

(1) In winter the north-east trade winds blow from land to sea, so they are dry over most of India. (2) But a part of these winds blows over the Bay of Bengal, gathers moisture and then strikes the Tamil Nadu coast, giving it winter rainfall. (Tamil Nadu also lies in the rain-shadow of the south-west monsoon, so most of its rain comes in this season.)

or: How does the wind system influence the climate of India during different seasons?

(1) In winter, north-east winds blow from land to sea, so they are cold and dry and most of India has a dry season (except the Tamil Nadu coast). (2) In summer, low pressure over the land draws moist south-west winds from the sea, which bring widespread rain from June to September. (3) Jet streams bring western disturbances in winter, and land–sea breezes and local winds like the loo affect daily weather.

sa: Describe any three factors affecting the climate of India.

(1) Latitude: the Tropic of Cancer divides India into a hotter tropical south and a sub-tropical north. (2) Distance from the sea: coastal places have an equable climate, interior places an extreme climate. (3) Mountains: the Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds and trap the monsoon; the Western Ghats cause heavy rain on their windward side. (Altitude, surface winds and jet streams also matter.)

Explain any three reasons for the uneven distribution of rainfall in India.

(1) Relief: the Western Ghats and north-eastern hills force winds to rise and give heavy rain on windward sides, while leeward areas like the Deccan are rain-shadow areas. (2) Distance from the sea: rain decreases from the coast to the interior and from east to west along the northern plains as winds lose moisture. (3) The Aravallis lie parallel to the Arabian Sea branch, so western Rajasthan gets very little rain.

Describe any three main features of the hot weather season in India.

(1) From March to May temperatures rise in the plains, west and central India, and a low-pressure monsoon trough forms from Jaisalmer to Odisha. (2) Hot, dry winds called 'loo' blow over the northern plains and dust storms occur in the north-west. (3) Local thunderstorms — Kaal Baisakhi in West Bengal — and pre-monsoon mango showers in Kerala and Karnataka occur.

Describe any three characteristics of the cold weather season in India.

(1) It lasts from December to February; temperature decreases from south to north and frost occurs in the north-west. (2) North-east trade winds blow from land to sea, so it is mostly dry with clear skies — except the Tamil Nadu coast, which gets winter rain. (3) Western disturbances give light rain in the north-west, useful for rabi crops, and snowfall on the Himalayas.

la: Explain the mechanism of the monsoon and describe the advancing south-west monsoon season.

Mechanism: (1) In summer north-west India becomes very hot, creating a low-pressure monsoon trough from Jaisalmer to Balasore, while the Indian Ocean is cooler with high pressure. (2) Winds therefore blow from the ocean to the land from the south-west — a reversal of the winter north-east winds — carrying moisture. Advancing monsoon: (3) The winds reach the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in late May and Kerala in the first week of June with a 'burst'. (4) The Arabian Sea branch gives heavy rain on the western slopes of the Western Ghats, reaches Mumbai by 10 June, and leaves the Deccan in rain-shadow. (5) The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the north-east and West Bengal and turns west along the plains, rain decreasing westwards (Kolkata 120 cm, Delhi 56 cm). (6) The whole country is covered by mid-July; there are wet and dry spells, floods and droughts.
How are the seasons related to the socio-cultural and economic life of India? What is the impact of global warming?

(1) India's agro-based economy follows the seasons — kharif crops with the monsoon, rabi in winter, zaid at the end of winter. (2) Diet and clothing change with seasons — woollens and calorie-rich food in winter, juicy fruits and drinks in summer. (3) Festivals coincide with seasons and harvests: Makar Sankranti, Lohri, Pongal, Basant Panchami, Holi, Baisakhi, Onam, Dussehra, Durga Puja and Diwali. (4) Floods and droughts in the monsoon hamper the economy. (5) Global warming — caused by CO2 and CFCs from industry, vehicles and deforestation — is disturbing the cycle of seasons. (6) Since about 70% of Indians depend on agriculture, rising temperatures and irregular rain can seriously harm food production and livelihoods.
